messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Jamal, a 50-year-old African American plumber, came to treatment after months in which a single assault had come to organize his days. He had been walking from his truck to a row house job in a neighborhood he knew well when two men came up behind him, one grabbing his shoulder and the other reaching into his tool bag. The struggle was brief but brutal: the jolt of a hand on his back, the sight of a face rushing close, the metallic flash of a wrench dropping to the pavement. What stayed with Jamal was not a clear story he could tell, but pieces that hit him later as if they were happening again — the image of the alley wall, the angle of a forearm, the look in one man’s eyes. He kept saying he could not put it into words, only that he felt sick with guilt when he thought about it, as if he should have seen it coming or done something different. Since then, he has been unable to shake the conviction that he is no longer the man his work used to prove him to be. Plumbing had defined him for decades: carrying his own equipment, sizing up a problem, fixing what others could not. Now he finds himself thinking he is no longer capable of doing those things, and that what happened was deeply unfair and has simply been allowed to stand. That sense of injustice sits beside a deeper self-doubt, a fear that he cannot trust himself to do the right thing if danger ever appears again.

Those beliefs have narrowed his world. Jamal says he only feels safe in a very limited number of places, and the list is shrinking. He is most settled in his own house, in the bedroom with the door locked, or sitting beside his wife in the living room at night with the television on low. Everywhere else feels precarious, especially the sites where he works. A small movement near him — a coworker turning suddenly with a pipe, a passerby stepping around the truck, someone approaching too quickly in a stairwell — makes him react as if he is in danger before he has time to think. He stiffens, scans, and starts measuring exits. His own thoughts fuel that vigilance: because he believes he is less capable and cannot trust his judgment, he feels he has to be on guard all the time, as though vigilance might compensate for what he sees as his failure. At work, that leaves him tense and distracted, checking the street instead of focusing on the repair, and he has begun choosing easier jobs or asking his supervisor to send another man when a building or block feels wrong to him. The result has been practical and painful; he is doing less of the work that once made him feel solid and useful.

The more he tries to keep danger away, the more the memory seems to break into him in fragments. When he catches sight of a dropped tool, a narrow passage between buildings, or the quick movement of someone coming up close behind him, the assault returns as pictures rather than a narrative. He sees the wall, the shoulder, the hand, the gleam of metal, but the event never settles into words. And each time those images surge back, the same guilt follows, vivid and immediate, and his body seems to learn that the world is unsafe all over again. That renewed alarm pulls him back into the very narrow spaces where he feels protected, reinforcing the sense that only a few places are safe enough. Even at home, sleep has become difficult; he lies awake listening, startled by movement in the house or outside, his body tensing before he can decide whether there is any real threat. His wife has noticed him sleeping in short stretches and waking at the slightest sound, but Jamal mostly keeps to himself, embarrassed by how much energy it takes just to get through an ordinary day.

He finally sought help after a morning when he froze on a jobsite because a young man hurried past him carrying a ladder, and Jamal felt his whole body brace as if the assault were starting again. He went home early and sat in the truck for a long time before going inside, frightened by how small his world had become and how little confidence he had left in himself. What he most fears now is that he will keep living this way — alert, cornered, and unsure of his own judgment — and what he most hopes for is to feel safe enough again to work, sleep, and move through the city without every movement around him warning him of danger.

violation_explanations: The vignette shows Jamal’s negative beliefs and self-doubt, but it does not clearly state that these appraisals directly create or intensify his sense of threat.
The traumatic memory is described as intrusive and distressing, but the vignette does not explicitly connect the memory to an increased sense of threat.
The vignette describes threat-like feelings and hypervigilance around reminders, but it does not clearly say that the sense of threat causes the memory to recur or intrude.
